title: Isolation Precautions
body:
## Precaution types

| Type | PPE | Room | Key organisms |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Standard** | Hand hygiene always. Gloves for any contact with blood, body fluids, mucous membranes or non-intact skin. Gown, mask and eye protection whenever a splash is possible | Any | Applies to **every patient, every time**, diagnosis unknown |
| **Contact** | Gown and gloves on entry | Private room or cohort with like patients; dedicated equipment | MRSA, VRE, ESBL and CRE, scabies, lice, impetigo, draining wounds, RSV, uncontained abscess |
| **Contact-plus / enteric (spores)** | Gown and gloves; **soap-and-water** hand washing; sporicidal cleaning | Private room with a dedicated toilet | *C. difficile*, norovirus |
| **Droplet** | Surgical mask on entry (droplets travel roughly `3–6 ft`); eye protection when splashing is likely | Private room; door may stay open | Influenza, pertussis, *Neisseria meningitidis*, group A strep (first `24 h` of therapy), mumps, rubella, diphtheria |
| **Airborne** | Fit-tested `N95` or PAPR | Airborne infection isolation room: negative pressure, `6–12` air changes per hour, **door closed** | Tuberculosis, measles, varicella and disseminated zoster (also contact), SARS-CoV-2 per facility policy |
| **Special / high-consequence** | Impermeable coverall or gown, double gloves, boot and head covers, full face shield or PAPR, with a **trained observer** for donning and doffing | Dedicated AIIR with an anteroom | Viral hemorrhagic fevers (Ebola, Marburg), novel respiratory pathogens |
| **Protective environment** (reverse) | PPE protects the *patient* | Positive pressure, HEPA filtration, `12` or more air changes per hour; no fresh flowers or plants | Allogeneic stem-cell transplant, profound neutropenia |

Airborne and contact stack: varicella, disseminated zoster and measles patients get both. Mask the **patient** with a surgical mask any time they leave the room.

## Donning order

1. Hand hygiene
2. Gown — tie at the neck and waist
3. Mask or `N95` respirator — mold the nosepiece, then do a user seal check
4. Goggles or face shield
5. Gloves — pull over the gown cuffs

## Doffing order

1. **Gloves** first — they are the dirtiest
2. Goggles or face shield, handling only the band at the back
3. Gown — roll it away from you, contaminated side in
4. Hand hygiene
5. Leave the room, close the door, **then** remove the mask or respirator by the straps from behind
6. Hand hygiene again

> **Key:** The respirator comes off **outside** the room. Taking an `N95` off inside an airborne room undoes the entire shift's worth of protection.

## Hand hygiene: which agent

| Situation | Agent |
|---|---|
| Routine, hands not visibly soiled | Alcohol-based rub, `60–95%` alcohol. Rub all surfaces `20 s` or until dry |
| Hands visibly soiled or greasy | Soap and water, at least `20 s` of scrubbing |
| *C. difficile*, other spore formers, norovirus | **Soap and water only** — alcohol does not kill spores, it just moves them around |
| Before eating, after the restroom | Soap and water |

The five moments: before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body-fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, after touching the patient's surroundings.

## Needlestick and exposure

1. Wash the site with soap and water immediately. Flush eyes or mucous membranes with water or saline for `15 min`. Do **not** squeeze the wound, and do not pour bleach or antiseptic into it.
2. Report to your supervisor right away — do not finish the shift first.
3. Go to Employee Health or the ED per facility policy.
4. Identify the source patient; rapid HIV, HBV and HCV testing on the source, with consent per state law.
5. Baseline testing on you.
6. **HIV PEP: start as soon as possible, ideally within `1–2 hours` and no later than `72 hours`.** A `28-day`, three-drug course.
7. **HBV:** if you are unvaccinated or a known non-responder, hepatitis B immune globulin plus vaccine, ideally within `24 hours`, and no later than `7 days`.
8. **HCV:** no prophylaxis exists. Baseline plus HCV RNA at `3–6 weeks` and antibody at `4–6 months`; acute infection is treated if it appears.
9. Follow-up testing at `6 weeks`, `12 weeks` and `6 months` (a `4th-generation` assay can close out at `4 months`).
10. The event goes on the OSHA sharps injury log.

> **On shift:** The clock on HIV prophylaxis starts at the stick, not at the end of your shift. Every hour of delay costs efficacy.

## C. difficile cleaning

Soap and water for hands, every time. Clean the room and all equipment with an **EPA-registered sporicidal agent**, usually a `1:10` bleach dilution (about `5000 ppm` sodium hypochlorite), with the contact time the label states. Dedicate the blood pressure cuff, stethoscope and thermometer to that room. Precautions continue at least until `48 hours` after the diarrhea resolves — many facilities keep them until discharge.

## Wristband colors

| Color | Usual meaning |
|---|---|
| Red | Allergy |
| Yellow | Fall risk |
| Purple | Do not resuscitate / limited resuscitation |
| Pink | Restricted extremity — no blood pressure, no draws, no IV |
| Green | Latex allergy (some systems) |

> **Trap:** Band colors **vary by hospital and by state**, and some systems reuse the same color for different meanings. Read the printed word on the band; never act on the color alone.
